rv.q: Yet this is also a thrillingly inventive and entertaining night at the theater.
One of its strengths is that it’s not agitprop, but nor is it passive entertainment; the double-edge of its droll, old-time showbizzy treatment of a shocking true story gives the musical real teeth.
The show is stuffed with bravura, impassioned, individual performances that fuse into an inestimably powerful ensemble.
Ultimately, alas, the songs aren't tough or surprising enough to take us beyond contrasts of tragedy and minstrelsy.
This bold musical keeps you tapping your feet while it socks you with an emotional punch to the gut.
The show's creators have fashioned a work that is at once devastatingly sad and buoyantly entertaining.
The result is a show that is both deeply serious and surprisingly entertaining.
Perhaps with a more nuanced book and flexible frame, Scottsboro would have more punch.

The musical never really resolves the tension between its impulse to entertain us with hoary jokes and quivering tambourines and the desire to render the harsh morals of its story with earnest insistence.
It’s still smashing, and it’s still shocking.
This is the best new musical of the year.

'The Scottsboro Boys' sets a high bar for Broadway musicals this season.
Kander and Ebb's score is exceptional.
In the end, it's a show that leaves you disturbed, entertained and just a little bit prouder of Broadway.
And while the result is thoughtful, vibrant entertainment, the earnestness and irreverence can seem self-conscious.
But for most of the evening, the adventurous show doesn't fit its parts together very well.
This stratagem fails because the juxtaposition defuses both gestures, just as the minstrel-style heartiness defuses the historical agony.

The unerring expertise in writing, staging, design and performance that makes this show so exciting is a striking reminder how musicals crafted well in the classic Broadway style remain more satisfying.
